volumes.title: The Hay Meadows at Fellfoot
volumes.text:
I am Tamsin Arkwright, schoolmistress of Emberwick, and this summer I mean to walk from the foot of the Northern Fells to the top of Cold Cap, writing down every plant I can name. My companion is a donkey called Pudding, who carries the press, the blotting paper and the kettle, and has opinions about all three.

We begin in the hay meadows at Fellfoot, early in June, before the scythes. Wood cranesbill stands knee-high and violet-blue among the buttercups. Yellow rattle is everywhere; it steals from the roots of the grasses and keeps them short, which is why the flowers have room. Shake a ripe pod and it rattles like a tiny purse.

My grandfather walked this way forty years ago. His notebook ends with one line: 'Least willow, Cold Cap summit. Smallest tree in the world.' I should like to see it.

volumes.title: The Beck Side
volumes.text:
Second week of June. Pudding the donkey and I have left the Fellfoot meadows and are following Rushy Beck upstream, which is the lazy way to climb the Northern Fells: the water has already found the easiest road.

The banks are a garden nobody planted. Marsh marigold is nearly over, its gold cups gone to green stars of seed. Water avens hangs its dusky pink heads as if shy. Where the ground squelches there is lady's smock, pale lilac, and brooklime with small blue flowers sitting right in the stream.

I tasted the brooklime, since the old herbals call it a salad. It is bitter enough to make a schoolmistress pull a face. Pudding ate the rest and seemed to think me fussy. I, Tamsin Arkwright, pressed four sheets today. The blotting paper is already running short, and we are barely above the last farm.

volumes.title: The Gill Wood
volumes.text:
Rushy Beck climbs into a steep wooded ravine, which the people of the Northern Fells call a gill. I, Tamsin Arkwright, went in on foot. Pudding the donkey declined and waited at the gate.

It is cool and green inside, all oak and birch and hazel, with the beck talking loudly below. The bluebells are finished, but wood sorrel still covers the banks, each leaf three folded hearts. The leaves close in rain and at night, like small umbrellas being put away. Higher up, bilberry makes a low thicket hung with pink lantern flowers, and sweet woodruff grows in whorls like tiny green wheels.

I found wild garlic by smell before sight. The whole upper wood reeks of it, pleasantly, as a kitchen does. I counted nineteen flowering plants without leaving the path, and came out with wet knees and a new respect for shade.

volumes.title: Walls and Intake Fields
volumes.text:
Above the gill wood the Northern Fells are parcelled into intake fields, rough pastures taken in from the moor long ago and fenced with drystone walls. No mortar holds them, only patience. Pudding the donkey and I followed one wall for two miles at the end of June.

A wall is a cliff that someone has kindly built at eye level. Stonecrop sits on the capstones with yellow stars. Wall pennywort pokes round green coins from the cracks, and herb robert, red-stemmed, grows wherever a spoonful of soil has blown in. On the shady side, foxgloves stand taller than the donkey.

I watched a bumblebee work a foxglove from the bottom bell upward. The lowest flowers open first, so she always climbs. A shepherd named Ned Tolliver, mending a gap, told me the walls are older than the church. The plants seem to agree.

volumes.title: The Heather Moor
volumes.text:
We are through the last gate. Hagg Moor lies open on every side, and for the first time since Fellfoot there is no wall, no tree and no shade. It is July. I, Tamsin Arkwright, have tied my hat on with string.

Three heathers grow here, and it took me a morning to tell them apart. Ling is the common one, with tiny scale leaves and pale flowers still in bud. Bell heather has fat crimson bells and likes dry banks. Cross-leaved heath is rose pink, with leaves in fours like a cross, and keeps to the wet hollows. Learn which is underfoot and you know whether your boots will stay dry.

Bilberries are ripening among them. Pudding the donkey has a purple muzzle and no remorse. Mine is no better, and there is nobody up here to mind.

volumes.title: Mirk Moss
volumes.text:
Beyond Hagg Moor the ground gives up being ground. This is Mirk Moss, a blanket bog a mile across, and I crossed it in mid-July by stepping exactly where Ned Tolliver the shepherd told me to step. Pudding the donkey went round by the cart track, sensibly.

Bog moss holds the whole place together, a wet sponge of red and green many feet deep. Cotton grass nods white tufts over it, and is a sedge, neither cotton nor grass. Bog asphodel stands in yellow spikes. On the bare peat I found sundew, no bigger than a penny, its red leaves fringed with sticky drops.

I watched a midge land on one. It did not leave. The leaf folds slowly over its catch and takes a meal the poor soil cannot give it. I felt some sympathy for the plant. The midges have been dining on me all week.

volumes.title: The Limestone Pavement
volumes.text:
High on the Northern Fells, above Mirk Moss, the peat stops and a floor of pale grey rock begins. Whitescar is a limestone pavement: flat blocks, called clints, split by deep cracks, called grikes. From a distance it looks as bare as a scrubbed doorstep.

Look down a grike and it is another matter. Each crack is a narrow, sheltered garden, safe from wind and sheep. Hart's-tongue fern hangs in green straps. Wild thyme spills over the edges. In one grike, an arm's length down, I found bloody cranesbill in full magenta flower, and lily of the valley leaves beside it: woodland plants living in a cellar.

Pudding the donkey will not set a hoof on the clints. I went alone, on hands and knees, peering into cracks like a woman who has dropped a ring. It is late July, and I, Tamsin Arkwright, have filled the second press.

volumes.title: Lantern Tarn
volumes.text:
A tarn is a small mountain lake, and Lantern Tarn lies in a hollow under Raven Crag, cold and clear as window glass. Pudding the donkey and I camped beside it for three days at the start of August, the longest we have stopped since Fellfoot.

Bogbean grows in the shallows, its three-part leaves held above the water like broad beans that have lost their way. The fringed pink-and-white flowers are over, though I found one late spike. Farther out, water lobelia sends thin stalks up through the surface, each with a few pale lilac flowers nodding over its own reflection. The leaves stay on the bottom in neat rosettes.

To see those I took off my boots and waded. The cold made my ankles ache within a minute. I sketched standing in the water anyway, and afterwards said some words that I do not teach.

volumes.title: Scree and Crag
volumes.text:
Raven Crag stands over Lantern Tarn, and below it lies a long fan of broken stone. This is scree. It slides when trodden on, so I, Tamsin Arkwright, crossed it slowly in August with a stick, having left the donkey at the tarn.

Parsley fern is the plant of the scree: bright green tufts that look just like the kitchen herb and grow where nothing else will hold. On the crag itself, out of reach of sheep, the ledges are crowded. Roseroot hangs in thick grey-green bunches; break the root and it smells of roses. Alpine lady's mantle has leaves edged and backed with silver silk. Mountain sorrel has kidney-shaped leaves, sharp and pleasant to chew.

Everything here is small, tough and close to the rock. I am beginning to resemble the flora. Nine weeks out, and my grandfather's summit is the next thing above me.

volumes.title: The Wet Ledges
volumes.text:
On the north face of Cold Cap, a morning's climb above Raven Crag, water seeps from the rock all summer. It was mid-August when I reached these ledges, and I had to tie Pudding the donkey to a boulder and go on without her.

The saxifrages live here. Their name means stone-breaker, though they only use cracks the frost has made. Starry saxifrage has white petals, each with two yellow dots, on stalks as thin as thread. Yellow mountain saxifrage makes mats along every trickle. Beside them grows moss campion, a tight green cushion that is no moss at all, studded with pink flowers. A cushion as wide as a dinner plate may be older than I am.

I lay on my front to draw it, with cold water running into one sleeve. A raven watched from above and made a remark. I chose to take it as encouragement.

volumes.title: The Summit of Cold Cap
volumes.text:
The top of Cold Cap is a stony plateau where the wind never quite stops. I, Tamsin Arkwright, came up on the twentieth of August with my grandfather's notebook in my pocket. Pudding the donkey, to my surprise, came too.

At first I saw only grey woolly moss and stiff sedge. Then I knelt. Flat against the ground, between the stones, lay round shining leaves no bigger than my little fingernail, with a few fluffy seed-heads among them. Least willow. Its trunk and branches creep under the moss, and only the twig tips show. The whole tree would fit under a teacup.

So he was right, forty years ago, and it is still here. I did not pick any. I drew it life size, which took very little paper, and wrote the date beneath his. Then I sat beside the smallest tree in the world and ate an apple.

volumes.title: Down Before the Frost
volumes.text:
We came down from Cold Cap in the first week of September, Pudding the donkey and I, by the road we went up: ledges, crag, tarn, pavement, bog, moor, walls, gill, beck. Everything had moved on without us. The ling on Hagg Moor was in full purple flower and humming with bees. The foxgloves were brown rattling poles. At Fellfoot the meadows were shorn and green again.

There was frost on the grass the morning we reached the village. I counted the pressed sheets on the inn table: two hundred and six plants, from wood cranesbill to least willow.

They go to Emberwick Library with this book. School opens on Monday, and Miss Arkwright must be back at her desk. Pudding has been promised a winter of doing nothing. I have added a line to my grandfather's notebook, under his: 'Still there. Go and see.'

volumes.title: The Churchyard Wall
volumes.text:
My name is Lettice Brambling, of Tanner's Row, Emberwick. On New Year's Day I resolved to find and name one hundred kinds of moss within a day's journey of my own door, and to finish by the year's end. My tools are a hand lens that was my late husband's, a penknife, and a great many paper packets.

January is a good month to begin. Mosses have no dislike of cold, and with the flowers gone there is nothing else to look at. I started at the churchyard wall. Wall screw-moss grows on the mortar in neat green cushions, each leaf ending in a white hair. Its capsules stand up on stalks like tiny candle-snuffers.

Under the lens a cushion becomes a forest. I stayed until my feet were numb and the verger asked if I had lost something. Nine kinds by teatime.

volumes.title: Roofs and Cushions
volumes.text:
February, and I have been looking up. Every old roof in Emberwick carries moss, and from the lane behind the bakery I can study a whole slope of tiles without a ladder. I am Lettice Brambling, and my neighbours have stopped asking.

The round grey pincushions are grey-cushioned grimmia. Long white leaf-hairs give them a frosted look. When a cushion dries it turns hoary and tight; a shower later it is green and soft again. The capsules curve back down into the cushion on bent stalks, as if tucking themselves in.

A moss capsule is a seed-box without seeds. It holds spores, fine as flour. Around its mouth is a ring of teeth that open in dry air and close in damp, so the spores go out only on a good day for flying. I made them move by breathing on one. Seventeen kinds now, toward my hundred.

volumes.title: The Woodland Floor
volumes.text:
In March I, Lettice Brambling, took my lens to Coppice Bank, the oak wood above Emberwick mill, before the leaves came and shut out the light.

The woodland floor is where mosses grow large. Common haircap stands a hand high in dark green stars, each stem like a small fir tree; lie down beside a patch and you are in a pine forest fit for beetles. Swan's-neck thyme-moss carries its capsules on curved red stalks, exactly as named. Over the logs and tree-foots run the feather mosses, branched like ferns and soft as fur.

A moss has no true roots. It holds on by fine threads and drinks through its leaves, straight from rain and mist, which is why a wet wood suits it. I came home with thirty-one kinds in the book and a great deal of the wood on my coat.

volumes.title: Stones in the Ember
volumes.text:
April brought rain, and the river Ember ran high and brown under the mill bridge at Emberwick. When it dropped I went down the bank with my skirts pinned up, a walking stick, and my hand lens on a string.

Some mosses live under water altogether. Greater water-moss grows on the stones in dark tresses a foot long, streaming in the current like hair. Its leaves are folded into keels, in three rows along each stem. On the splashed rocks just above the waterline sit tight dark cushions that are drowned in every flood and seem none the worse.

I wanted a piece from midstream. A boy called Wilf Tarrow, fishing for minnows, waded out and fetched it for a penny, then stayed to look through the lens. He says the cushions are forests and the water-moss is a mermaid. Forty kinds. I, Lettice Brambling, have an assistant.

volumes.title: The Old Orchard Trunks
volumes.text:
May in Emberwick, and the orchard behind Tanner's Row is all blossom. Everyone else looks up at it. Wilf Tarrow and I, Lettice Brambling, look at the trunks.

Bark is a country of its own. On the old apple trees, cypress-leaved plait-moss lies in flat green mats, each shoot neatly braided. Wood bristle-moss makes small dark tufts, with capsules half hidden among the leaves and wearing hairy pointed caps. The caps fall off when the spores are ready, like hats at a wedding.

Mosses do the tree no harm. They take nothing from it but a place to sit. Wilf, who is nine, asked whether moss always grows on the north side. We walked round six trees with a compass. It grows wherever it is damp, which is often north and just as often not. Fifty-two kinds, and we are past halfway.

volumes.title: Bog Moss on the Marsh
volumes.text:
On Midsummer Eve I, Lettice Brambling, went out on the marsh below Emberwick in borrowed boots, with Wilf Tarrow carrying the basket. We wanted bog moss, and the marsh has more of it than anything else.

Bog moss grows in soft hummocks, pale green, ochre and wine red, each colour a different kind. Every stem ends in a shaggy head like a small mop. Most of the plant is empty cells, made for holding water. Wilf squeezed a handful and filled a teacup. At home we weighed a dry tuft, soaked it and weighed it again: twenty times heavier.

It builds its own ground, growing at the top while the bottom turns slowly to peat. The old people here used it dried to line cradles. Seven kinds of bog moss, and seven more from the ditches, bring the book to sixty-six. My stockings may not recover.

volumes.title: The Dry Month
volumes.text:
Hardly a drop of rain fell on Emberwick in July. The mosses on the churchyard wall shrivelled to grey-brown crusts. I, Lettice Brambling, found two new kinds in the first week and none after, and the count stuck at sixty-eight.

So I tried an experiment instead. I took a cushion of wall screw-moss, dry as a biscuit, set it on a saucer on the kitchen table, and let one drop of water fall on it. Under the lens the leaves untwisted and spread while I watched. In two minutes the cushion was green. Wilf Tarrow timed it with my husband's watch.

A moss does not die of drought. It stops, like a clock nobody has wound, and starts again when it is wet. I have a packet in my drawer collected in January. We wetted that too, and it opened just the same. I find this cheering, at my age.

volumes.title: Mr. Dobbin's Lawn
volumes.text:
My neighbour in Tanner's Row, Emberwick, Mr. Dobbin, wages war on the moss in his lawn. Every August evening I hear the rake. I, Lettice Brambling, went round to ask for the rakings, and he gave me a look I shall treasure.

His enemy is springy turf-moss. Each shoot has leaves bent sharply back, so from above it looks like a row of tiny green stars. It likes shade, damp and short grass, and Mr. Dobbin supplies all three by mowing close under his own apple tree. I told him so. He was not grateful.

Raking only helps it. Every broken scrap can grow into a new plant, so he sows it as he goes. In his barrowful Wilf Tarrow and I found five kinds, two of them new to the book. Seventy. Mr. Dobbin has asked, stiffly, to borrow the lens.

volumes.title: The Rotten Log
volumes.text:
September, and Coppice Bank above Emberwick smells of mushrooms. A fallen oak lies near the top path, so soft now that a finger goes into it. I, Lettice Brambling, spent two afternoons on that single log.

The prize was four-toothed moss, which has a trick. At the tips of some shoots sit small green cups, each holding a few loose grains like eggs in a nest. A raindrop landing in the cup splashes them out, and every grain can grow a new plant. Wilf Tarrow did the raindrop's work with a wet straw and flicked them a full hand-span.

Beside it grow the liverworts, flat and leafy, the mosses' quiet cousins. I am putting them in an appendix; a compendium ought to be generous. One log gave eleven new mosses. Eighty-one in all, with three months left. I begin to think it can be done.

volumes.title: A Day on the Fells
volumes.text:
A day's journey from my door, I said in January, and in October I, Lettice Brambling, used every hour of it. The carrier took Wilf Tarrow and me from Emberwick to Fellfoot at dawn, and we climbed to the edge of Hagg Moor in the Northern Fells.

The fell mosses are a different company. Woolly fringe-moss covers the boulders in grey fleeces. Under the heather grows glittering wood-moss, the handsomest I have seen: red stems, with fronds set one above another like steps. Each step is one year's growth. Wilf counted seven on a single shoot, so that moss was two years younger than he is.

We found fourteen new kinds between the last wall and the first cairn. Ninety-five. I slept the whole way home in the cart, I am told, with a packet in each hand.

volumes.title: Goblin Gold
volumes.text:
The quarryman's wife told me of it in spring: a green-gold light at the back of the old slate level on Coppice Bank, which the children of Emberwick call goblin gold. In November, with ninety-eight kinds in the book, I, Lettice Brambling, went to look. Wilf Tarrow, my assistant, came too.

Ten paces into the tunnel, where daylight was nearly gone, the floor glowed. It was faint and greenish, like a cat's eye, and it vanished when I moved my head. I carried a thimbleful of earth out to the lens.

Luminous moss. The plant itself is a tiny pale feather. The glow comes from a film of green threads on the soil, whose round cells gather the last scrap of daylight and throw some back. It makes no light; it only wastes none. Ninety-nine. Wilf wanted it to be goblins, and was gracious about it.

volumes.title: The Hundredth Moss
volumes.text:
December in Emberwick, and I, Lettice Brambling, had ninety-nine mosses in the book and eleven days left. I walked the churchyard, the mill bridge and Coppice Bank again, and found only old friends. Wilf Tarrow searched the school roof and was sent down.

On the last morning of the year I sat on my own doorstep in Tanner's Row to lace my boots. Between the flagstones ran a thin line of silver-green, flattened by twelve months of my own feet. I fetched the lens. Silver-moss: tiny shoots like catkins, pale and shining, the commonest pavement moss there is. I had stepped over it every single day.

So the hundredth is the nearest. Wilf wrote the label himself. The compendium is bound in green cloth and goes to the library tomorrow, with a hundred packets in a box. Next year he wants lichens. I have asked for a week's rest first.

volumes.title: The Spring at Emberhead
volumes.text:
The river Ember begins as a cold trickle under a boulder, high in the Northern Fells, at a place called Emberhead. I am Clemency Oake, and I draw plants for a living. This May my nephew Pip and I set out to follow the Ember from its spring to the sea, drawing every fern on its banks, and every fern ally too.

The allies came first. In the short turf round the spring grows fir clubmoss, in stiff green fingers a few inches high. It is neither a fir nor a moss. Clubmosses, horsetails and quillworts are the ferns' old relations: like ferns they have no flowers and no seeds, and breed by spores as fine as dust.

Pip, who is eleven and carries the press, asked how a plant manages without seeds. I told him he would know by September. He has written that down, in case I forget.

volumes.title: Along the High Beck
volumes.text:
For its first few miles the Ember is only a beck, hopping down the fellside from Emberhead between banks of peat and rock. My nephew Pip and I walked it in the middle of May, when the new fronds were still soft.

Two ferns own these banks. Lemon-scented fern stands in pale yellow-green shuttlecocks; draw a frond through your fingers and it smells of lemon peel. Hard fern is darker and tougher, and has two sorts of frond on one plant. The low, spreading ones are plain leaves. The tall, thin ones in the middle, like fishbones, carry the spores.

Pip rubbed and sniffed every fern for a mile, to be certain, and by evening smelt like a pudding. I, Clemency Oake, drew both kinds with my feet on a stone in the water. The beck is already wide enough that we must choose a side and keep to it.

volumes.title: Skein Force
volumes.text:
Where the Ember leaves the high fells it drops sixty feet into a gorge, and the fall is called Skein Force. The air there is wet all year. My nephew Pip and I climbed down beside it in late May.

On the dripping rock behind the spray grows the filmy fern. I, Clemency Oake, had wanted to draw it for twenty years. The fronds are an inch or two long, dark green, and so thin that light comes through them as through green tissue paper: one cell thick. Out of the damp a frond shrivels within the hour, so it would never travel to my drawing table.

It had to be drawn where it grew. I sat in the spray for two hours under an umbrella, with Pip holding the paint box in his hat. The drawing is a little cockled. It is the best thing I have done.

volumes.title: The Oak Wood and the Jar
volumes.text:
Below Skein Force the river Ember runs through Hanging Oak Wood, and in early June the ferns there were still unrolling. Each new frond comes up coiled like the head of a fiddle. My nephew Pip counted forty in one clump of male fern.

Male fern and lady fern grow side by side, and were named by people who thought one sturdy and the other delicate. They are only neighbours. Turn a frond over in late summer and the difference is plain: male fern has round spore-dots, lady fern has curved ones like commas.

Pip wanted to see spores grow. In my folder was a frond pressed last autumn, and the paper under it was brown with shed dust. We tipped it on to damp peat in a jam jar and tied muslin over the top. I, Clemency Oake, promised nothing. The jar travels in his coat pocket.

volumes.title: The Bracken Bank
volumes.text:
Out of the wood, the Ember valley opens between steep banks, and every bank is bracken. In mid-June it stood as high as my nephew Pip's chin. I am Clemency Oake, and I had half a mind to leave it out of the book, being so common.

That would have been unjust. Bracken is the one fern that makes its own thicket. The fronds rise singly from a black stem that creeps underground for yards, so a whole hillside may be one plant. Cut a stalk across near the base and the brown veins make a pattern; Pip sees an oak tree in it, and I see a two-headed bird.

The farmers here cut it in autumn for winter bedding in the byres. We drew one frond, folded in three to fit the page, and walked on through the rest with our arms up.

volumes.title: The Mill Bridge Wall
volumes.text:
At Emberwick the river passes under the old mill bridge, and my nephew Pip and I stopped a week there at midsummer. I, Clemency Oake, spent most of it leaning over the parapet, to the concern of passers-by.

Three small ferns live in the mortar. Maidenhair spleenwort has a wiry black stalk with round green leaflets in pairs, like beads on a thread. Wall-rue is stubby and grey-green and looks more like a herb than a fern. Rustyback is the neatest: thick scalloped fronds, green above and covered beneath with rust-brown scales. In dry weather it curls up and shows only the rusty side, then opens again after rain.

They ask for nothing but lime and a crack. Pip's jam jar of spores sat on the inn windowsill all week, and on the last morning the peat had a faint green bloom, like the skin on a pond.

volumes.title: The Limestone Gorge
volumes.text:
South of Emberwick the river Ember has cut a narrow gorge through pale limestone, called the Clatter for the noise the water makes. It is shady and damp even at the start of July, when my nephew Pip and I walked through it.

Hart's-tongue fern hangs from every ledge. It is the one fern that a child draws correctly at the first attempt: a plain, glossy green strap, undivided, with a wavy edge. Turn it over and the spores lie in straight brown stripes, slanting out from the midrib like the marks on a ruler. Pip measured the longest frond at twenty-two inches.

Higher in the cracks grows brittle bladder-fern, small and lacy, with stalks that snap at a touch. I, Clemency Oake, snapped three before I learned to draw it without holding it. Each spore-dot wears a tiny pale hood, the bladder of its name.

volumes.title: Two Odd Ferns
volumes.text:
Below the gorge the Ember slows and winds through old water meadows. My nephew Pip and I crossed them in the middle of July, on hands and knees, because the two ferns that live there are easier to kneel on than to see.

Adder's-tongue is a single oval leaf with one green spike standing up inside it. Moonwort is smaller still: a stalk with half-moon leaflets down each side, and a branched spike of spores like a bunch of tiny grapes. Neither unrolls from a coil as other ferns do. Country people say moonwort will open locks and pull the shoes off horses.

We tested this on the carrier's mare, with his leave. She kept all four shoes and ate the daisies. I, Clemency Oake, record the result for science. Pip found eleven moonworts. I found two, and the heel of my hand found a thistle.

volumes.title: The Marsh and the Green Hearts
volumes.text:
Where the Lowlands sink toward the marsh, the Ember spreads into ditches and reed beds, and the ferns grow large. It was August. My nephew Pip and I went by punt, which he poled with more spirit than direction.

Royal fern stands on the ditch banks in clumps taller than I am. Its spores are not on the back of the leaves. They sit at the top of the frond in rusty tassels, like a plant in flower. Marsh fern creeps through the wet ground between, sending up thin pale fronds one at a time.

And in the jam jar that Pip has carried since the oak wood in June, the green film has become a crowd of flat green hearts, each smaller than a lentil. I, Clemency Oake, explained that these are not ferns yet. A fern grows up in two stages, and this is the first.

volumes.title: Horsetails on the Dyke
volumes.text:
Along the marsh dyke south of the reed beds, the river Ember is edged with horsetails, and in late August my nephew Pip and I walked a mile between them. They are fern allies, and the oddest of the family.

A horsetail is built in joints, like a fishing rod. Each hollow green stem pulls apart with a small pop and fits back together, and at every joint stands a ring of thin branches. Water horsetail grows in the ditch itself. Great horsetail, on the damp bank, reaches Pip's shoulder on ivory-white stems. They feel harsh because they are full of fine grit, and kitchen maids once scoured pewter with them.

Their ancestors were trees. The coal in the grate is partly made of horsetails and clubmosses as tall as church towers. I, Clemency Oake, find that a steadying thought. Pip took one to pieces and could not rebuild it.

volumes.title: The Quiet Pool
volumes.text:
A mile from the sea the Ember passes a shallow pool on Saltway Common. My nephew Pip and I came to it in September, looking for the last two inland plants on our list. One is a fern and one a fern ally, and nobody would take either for anything but grass.

Pillwort, the fern, creeps over the wet mud in thin green threads. Each new leaf unrolls from a tiny coil, and at the base sit hard brown pills the size of peppercorns, which hold the spores. Quillwort, the ally, grows right under the water in stiff dark tufts, like a bundle of quill pens. Pip fetched one with his sleeve rolled up.

I, Clemency Oake, drew them both life size, and both looked like lawn clippings. It cannot be helped. The honest dull ones belong in the book as much as the royal fern does.

volumes.title: Sea Spleenwort
volumes.text:
The river Ember ends at the Grey Coast, sliding out between two low cliffs into the sea. My nephew Pip and I reached it at the end of September, four months and sixty miles from the spring at Emberhead.

One fern was left. In a cleft of the cliff, wet with salt spray, grows sea spleenwort: glossy, leathery fronds, bright green against black rock. It is the only fern on our list that can bear salt. I, Clemency Oake, drew it at low tide with a wave filling my boots.

That makes thirty-one ferns and nine allies. And in Pip's jam jar, among the green hearts, one has put up a single true frond, no bigger than a clover leaf. Spore, heart, fern: he has his answer, as promised in May. He carried the jar home on his knees in the cart, and would not let me hold it.

volumes.title: Twelve Circles
volumes.text:
My uncle Ambrose left me Latchet Orchard, on the edge of Emberwick, and a map of it drawn on the back of a seed bill. The map shows twelve circles in three rows of four. None has a name. I am Gideon Thrale, a retired schoolmaster, and I know the kings of six countries and not one fruit tree.

I counted in January, in the snow: eleven trees, and in the far corner a mossy stump where the twelfth should be.

My neighbour, Mrs. Ansty, leaned on the gate and named the first. The leaning tree nearest the lane is an Ember Codlin, a cooking apple older than she is. Its fruit buds are fat and downy, its leaf buds thin and flat. She showed me where to prune: cut out the dead, the diseased and the crossing, and then stop. I wrote 'Codlin' in the first circle.

volumes.title: Catkins on the Cobnut
volumes.text:
February at Latchet Orchard, Emberwick, and one of my uncle's unnamed trees has named itself. In the hedge corner stands a many-stemmed bush hung with yellow catkins, shaking loose a dust of pollen whenever the wind moves. Even I, Gideon Thrale, know a hazel.

Mrs. Ansty corrected me kindly. It is a cobnut, a hazel bred for bigger nuts. The catkins are the male flowers. The female ones are harder to find: a fat bud with a tuft of crimson threads at the tip, no bigger than a grain of rice. I needed my reading spectacles. Wind carries the pollen across, and by September each red tuft may be a cluster of nuts, if the squirrels permit.

'Cobnut' goes in the second circle. The twigs she had me save from pruning the old codlin lie in damp sand in the shed. I am told to wait for March.

volumes.title: Plum Blossom and a Graft
volumes.text:
Late March, and the first blossom at Latchet Orchard has opened on a small tree by the south wall: white flowers on bare twigs, before a single leaf. Mrs. Ansty says it is a gage, the sweetest sort of plum, and that it flowers too early for its own good. One hard frost now and there will be no fruit in August. I, Gideon Thrale, have been checking the weathercock hourly.

This was also grafting week. The twigs saved from the old Ember Codlin came out of their sand, and Mrs. Ansty brought a young rootstock. She cut both on a long slant, fitted one to the other so the green layers under the bark met, and bound them with twine and wax. A new tree, she says, with the old tree's fruit.

It looks like a stick tied to a stick. 'Gage' is in the third circle.

volumes.title: The Pear in Flower
volumes.text:
The tallest tree in Latchet Orchard stands straight up from the middle row like a church spire, and in April it turned white from top to bottom. Mrs. Ansty, my neighbour here in Emberwick, says it is a pear, and that my uncle's grandfather likely planted it. Pears outlive the people who plant them by several generations.

I, Gideon Thrale, went close to admire it. Pear blossom is handsome, white with dark red anthers, and smells faintly of fish. Nobody had warned me. The flies and beetles enjoy it, and the bees come regardless.

The bark is the other mark of a pear: grey and cracked into small squares, like the hide of some patient old animal. Apple bark flakes in plates; cherry bark peels in bands. I am learning to read trees with the leaves off and the leaves on. 'Pear' is in the fourth circle.

volumes.title: The Crab and the Bees
volumes.text:
May is apple blossom month at Latchet Orchard, Emberwick. The old Ember Codlin by the lane is pink and white, and so is a smaller, thornier tree in the next row that I, Gideon Thrale, had taken for a poor relation.

Mrs. Ansty set me right. It is a crab apple, and my uncle planted it on purpose. An apple tree sets little fruit with its own pollen; it needs a different apple flowering nearby, and bees to carry between them. A crab flowers long and freely, so one crab can serve a whole orchard. Its own fruit is small, hard and sour, and makes the best jelly there is.

I sat under it for an hour. Honeybees, bumblebees and a small ginger bee all went from crab to codlin and back. 'Crab' is in the fifth circle. Against the shed wall, the grafted stick has two leaves.

volumes.title: The Late Walnut
volumes.text:
One tree at Latchet Orchard, Emberwick, stayed bare so long this spring that I, Gideon Thrale, had the saw out. Mrs. Ansty took it from my hand. A walnut, she said, is always last to wake, and it has reason: its young leaves are bronze, tender and easily frosted.

By June it was in full leaf, the largest tree in the back row. Crush a leaf and it smells sharp and spicy, something like polish. Very little grows beneath a walnut, and people have long sat under one to keep the flies off.

The nuts are green now, the size of plums. Mrs. Ansty pickles some this week, while a needle still passes through them. They stain the fingers brown for a fortnight; hers are proof. 'Walnut' is in the sixth circle. Meanwhile the apples are dropping their smallest fruit, which I am told is normal.

volumes.title: Cherries and Blackbirds
volumes.text:
July, and the mystery tree by the well at Latchet Orchard has given itself away. Its bark is glossy red-brown, ringed with rough bands like stitching, and for two weeks it has been covered in dark red cherries. I, Gideon Thrale, have had perhaps a pound of them. The blackbirds of Emberwick have had the rest.

I tried a net, and caught myself. I tried a scarecrow in my uncle's hat, and a thrush sat on it. Mrs. Ansty says a tall cherry belongs to the birds and always has; one picks from a ladder at dawn and is thankful.

There is a kind of bargain in it. The birds carry the stones away and drop them, and that is how wild cherries come to stand in every hedge between here and the river. I wrote 'Cherry' in the seventh circle with a stained thumb, and left a print.

volumes.title: The Mulberry
volumes.text:
The oldest-looking tree at Latchet Orchard, Emberwick, is a low, leaning thing propped on a wooden crutch. Mrs. Ansty calls it the mulberry, and says it is the wisest tree here, because it never opens a leaf until the frosts are truly finished.

In August it fruits. The berries are like long dark raspberries, and they ripen a few at a time over weeks. They are too soft to carry to market, so one eats them where one stands. The juice is crimson and gets everywhere. I, Gideon Thrale, went to the library with purple cuffs.

Mrs. Ansty spreads an old sheet under the boughs and shakes them gently. We filled two bowls and ruined the sheet. 'Mulberry' is in the eighth circle. By the shed, the grafted codlin has a shoot as long as my forearm, and I have stopped calling it a stick.

volumes.title: Damsons in the Hedge
volumes.text:
I had counted the tree in the eastern hedge of Latchet Orchard as part of the hedge. In September it bent under small, oval, blue-black plums with a grey bloom on them, and Mrs. Ansty informed me that I, Gideon Thrale, owned a damson.

A damson is a plum that has never been spoilt by kindness. It is thorny, tough, half wild, and fruits well in years when the pampered gage by the south wall sulks. Eaten raw it puckers the mouth. Cooked with sugar it turns a deep red-purple and tastes richer than any plum I know.

We picked eighteen pounds in an afternoon. Emberwick smells of jam this week from one end to the other; every kitchen has a pan on. Mrs. Ansty counts the stones on to a plate afterwards, to be sure of them all. 'Damson' is in the ninth circle. Three to go.

volumes.title: The Russet and the Apple Loft
volumes.text:
October is picking month at Latchet Orchard, Emberwick. The old Ember Codlin came down first, by the basketful, for pies. But the tree beside it puzzled me: its apples are small, rough and brown-gold, like fruit knitted from sacking. I, Gideon Thrale, assumed a disease.

Mrs. Ansty laughed for some time. It is a russet, and the rough coat is its nature. She cut one. The flesh is cream-coloured, dry and sweet, with a taste like nuts. It is a keeping apple, hard at picking and best after a month in store.

An apple is ready when it comes away with a lift and a quarter turn. We laid them in my uncle's loft on slatted trays, none touching another, and I am to look them over every week and remove any that turn. The loft already smells wonderful. 'Russet' is in the tenth circle.

volumes.title: The Medlar After Frost
volumes.text:
The last standing tree without a name at Latchet Orchard is small and crooked, with long leaves that turned red and gold this November. Its fruit is odd: brown, round and flat-ended, with a crown of leafy points, like a rosehip grown too large. I, Gideon Thrale, bit one in October and regretted it for an hour.

It is a medlar, says Mrs. Ansty, and I was too early. Medlars are picked after the first frosts and laid in straw for some weeks until they soften and darken. The old word is bletting. They look ruined, and are then ready.

We tried the first today in her kitchen in Emberwick. One squeezes the pulp out with a spoon. It tastes like stewed apple with dates. 'Medlar' is in the eleventh circle. That leaves the stump in the corner, and no fruit to name it by.

volumes.title: The Twelfth Circle
volumes.text:
December at Latchet Orchard, Emberwick, a year since I first counted eleven trees and a stump. I, Gideon Thrale, asked Mrs. Ansty what the twelfth had been. An Ember Codlin, she said, twin to the one by the lane. It blew down the winter my uncle Ambrose turned eighty, and he never had the heart to replant.

So we knew what to do. The graft we made in March, from the old codlin's own twigs, stands waist-high now in its pot. We grubbed out the stump, dug a wide hole, spread the roots, and trod the soil firm. Mrs. Ansty drove the stake. I tied it.

It will be five years before it bears. I wrote 'Codlin, again' in the twelfth circle, and under the map, in my best schoolroom hand, the names of all twelve. Then we went indoors and ate a russet each from the loft.
